content:
Quick answer

Rheumatoid arthritis can begin with painful, swollen joints, stiffness after rest and tiredness. Small joints in the hands and feet are often affected, but symptoms differ. Persistent unexplained joint swelling needs prompt assessment. A GP can arrange tests and refer to rheumatology; blood tests should not hold up an urgent referral.

What to notice

Joint pain, swelling and stiffness may develop over weeks, although symptoms sometimes begin more quickly. Both sides of the body can be affected, but a perfectly symmetrical pattern is not required. Fatigue and feeling generally unwell can accompany joint symptoms. These signs do not establish a diagnosis by themselves.

What to tell the GP

Explain which joints are swollen, when symptoms began, how mornings and daily tasks are affected, and whether symptoms come and go. Mention symptoms even if pain is manageable or you have had a normal blood test. NICE recommends urgent specialist referral for persistent synovitis when small hand or foot joints, or more than one joint, are affected; delay in seeking help is another reason for urgency.

What three working days means

NICE quality standard QS33 sets a target for referral within three working days of presentation in primary care for suspected persistent synovitis affecting multiple joints or the small joints of the hands and feet. That is the referral target, not a guarantee that the specialist appointment will take place within three days. Do not wait six weeks before reporting persistent swelling.

While assessment is arranged

Ask your GP what pain relief and activity are suitable and how to seek help if symptoms change. Keep a short symptom record if useful. Do not start or stop prescription treatment based on this page. A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint, especially with illness or shivering, needs urgent GP or NHS 111 assessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment.
